title: Use `IntStream.rangeClosed` to generate a sequence of account numbers and to iterate a list by index (so you can pair each employee with its position). Explain `range` versus `rangeClosed`, `mapToObj`, and when index-based iteration is appropriate.
shortTitle: Generate account numbers and iterate by index using IntStream.rangeClosed
keyPoints: IntStream.rangeClosed(start, end) is an inclusive range that yields start through end, including end
IntStream.range(start, end) is exclusive and stops at end-1, which is ideal for list indices
mapToObj turns each primitive int into an object, for example building an account-number String
IntStream.range(0, list.size()) lets you iterate by index and pair each element with its position
Index-based iteration is appropriate when you need the position, not just the element
IntStream avoids autoboxing, so it is more efficient than Stream<Integer> for numeric work
Use rangeClosed when the upper bound is a real value (1 to 100) and range when it is a count or size

s1_definition.oneliner: IntStream.rangeClosed(1, n) produces an inclusive int sequence you map to account numbers with mapToObj, while IntStream.range(0, list.size()) gives exclusive indices to pair each element with its position.
s1_definition.profdef:
IntStream range methods produce a sequence of primitive ints without boxing.

- **IntStream.range(start, end)** – yields `start` up to `end - 1`, so `end` is excluded.
- **IntStream.rangeClosed(start, end)** – yields `start` up to `end`, so `end` is included.
- **mapToObj(IntFunction)** – converts each `int` into an object, turning an int stream into a `Stream<T>`.
- **Index iteration** – `IntStream.range(0, list.size())` gives valid indices `0 .. size-1` to access the list by position.
- **No boxing** – `IntStream` works on primitive `int`, avoiding the `Integer` wrapper overhead of `Stream<Integer>`.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, Rajesh opens a block of new savings accounts numbered from one to ten. rangeClosed(1, 10) is the clerk counting out account numbers and including the last one, ten, because account ten is a real account. When Priya hands him a list of employees to seat, Rajesh instead counts seat positions from zero up to but not including the number of employees, which is range(0, size), because there is no seat at position equal to the count. Inclusive when the end is a real thing, exclusive when the end is just how many there are.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  range vs rangeClosed

  IntStream.range(1, 5)          IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 5)
       │                              │
       ▼                              ▼
   1 2 3 4                        1 2 3 4 5
   (end 5 excluded)               (end 5 included)
```

```text
  Account numbers via rangeClosed + mapToObj

  rangeClosed(1, 5)
       │  mapToObj(i -> "ACC-" + pad(i))
       ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │ ACC-00001                 │
  │ ACC-00002                 │
  │ ACC-00003                 │
  │ ACC-00004                 │
  │ ACC-00005                 │
  └──────────────────────────┘
```

```text
  Index iteration pairs element with position

  employees = [ Rajesh , Priya , Pankaj ]
  index       =   0        1        2

  IntStream.range(0, size)   // 0,1,2  (NOT rangeClosed)
       │  mapToObj(i -> (i+1) + ". " + list.get(i))
       ▼
   1. Rajesh
   2. Priya
   3. Pankaj
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
At the National Bank of India, Rajesh opens a block of new savings accounts numbered one through ten. He uses `IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10)` because account ten is a real account and must be included, then `mapToObj` turns each number into a formatted account code like ACC-00010. The inclusive end is right when the upper bound is a genuine value.

When Priya hands him a list of employees to number, the situation flips. Now he counts positions with `IntStream.range(0, employees.size())`, which stops one before the size, because there is no element at index equal to the count. Using `rangeClosed` here would reach that missing index and throw `IndexOutOfBoundsException`. Exclusive when the end is merely a count, inclusive when it is a real value.

`mapToObj` is the bridge from primitive ints to objects. An `IntStream` holds plain ints, which keeps numeric work fast by avoiding the `Integer` wrapper, but to build Strings or model objects you call `mapToObj`, and the stream becomes a `Stream<T>`. For pure arithmetic, `IntStream` also hands you `sum`, `average`, and `max` directly.

Index iteration earns its place only when the position matters: numbering rows, pairing an element with its index, or walking two parallel lists together. When you only need the elements, a direct `for-each` or `list.stream()` is clearer and safer.

Remember one sentence: rangeClosed includes the end for real value bounds, range excludes it for list indices, and mapToObj turns each int into the object you really need.
